motion: This House believes that all forms of child labour must be abolished immediately and without exception.

vocab.definition: The lasting damage to a child’s physical growth, cognitive ability and emotional health caused by premature work.
vocab.example: Developmental harm from heavy labour leaves children permanently disadvantaged in education and adult life.

vocab.definition: The cycle in which children who work instead of studying grow up poor and raise the next generation in the same conditions.
vocab.example: Child labour locks families into intergenerational poverty by denying the next generation the skills needed to escape.

vocab.definition: Work that exposes children to dangerous machinery, toxic substances or extreme physical strain.
vocab.example: Hazardous exploitation in mines and factories is never justified by family need.

vocab.definition: The systematic denial of schooling that results when children are forced into full-time work.
vocab.example: Educational deprivation turns temporary economic pressure into lifelong lost opportunity.

vocab.definition: The shared guilt of societies and consumers who benefit from goods produced by child workers.
vocab.example: Buying cheap products made with child labour makes every consumer part of the moral complicity.

vocab.definition: The clear breach of a child’s fundamental entitlements to protection, education and play.
vocab.example: Any policy that tolerates child labour is a deliberate rights violation.

vocab.definition: The gradual wearing down of a child’s body through excessive work, leading to injury and early ageing.
vocab.example: Physical attrition is visible in the bent spines and damaged lungs of children in brick kilns.

vocab.definition: The permanent limitation of a child’s intellectual potential caused by malnutrition, exhaustion and lack of schooling.
vocab.example: Cognitive stunting from early labour leaves young people unable to compete in a modern economy.

vocab.definition: The structural failure of governments and markets to protect children because their labour is cheap and convenient.
vocab.example: Systemic indifference allows child labour to persist even when laws formally forbid it.

vocab.definition: The irreversible theft of the years that should be spent learning, playing and growing in safety.
vocab.example: No economic argument can restore a lost childhood once it has been taken.

phrases.phrase: No child should have to trade their future for today’s survival.
examples: No child should have to trade their future for today’s survival, yet millions are forced to do exactly that.
The motion rests on a simple principle: no child should have to trade their future for today’s survival.
We cannot call ourselves civilised while no child should have to trade their future for today’s survival remains a daily reality.

phrases.phrase: Child labour is not a solution to poverty; it is a cause of poverty.
examples: Child labour is not a solution to poverty; it is a cause of poverty that traps families for generations.
Every serious study shows that child labour is not a solution to poverty; it is a cause of poverty.
We must reject the false claim that child labour is not a solution to poverty; it is a cause of poverty.

phrases.phrase: A child’s place is in the classroom, not in the workplace.
examples: A child’s place is in the classroom, not in the workplace, and any policy that denies this is indefensible.
We will not rest until a child’s place is in the classroom, not in the workplace becomes universal practice.
The right to education means a child’s place is in the classroom, not in the workplace.

phrases.phrase: Economic necessity cannot justify the sacrifice of a generation.
examples: Economic necessity cannot justify the sacrifice of a generation to cheap labour.
History will not accept the argument that economic necessity cannot justify the sacrifice of a generation.
We refuse to accept that economic necessity cannot justify the sacrifice of a generation.

phrases.phrase: Tolerating child labour is a failure of moral courage.
examples: Tolerating child labour is a failure of moral courage by governments and consumers alike.
Every delay shows that tolerating child labour is a failure of moral courage.
We must name it clearly: tolerating child labour is a failure of moral courage.

phrases.phrase: The cheapest labour is the most expensive for society.
examples: The cheapest labour is the most expensive for society because it destroys human potential.
When we calculate true costs, the cheapest labour is the most expensive for society.
Short-term profits ignore that the cheapest labour is the most expensive for society.

idioms.idiom: rob a child of their future
idioms.definition: To take away the opportunities and development that belong to every young person.
examples: Forcing a child into full-time work is to rob a child of their future.
Every year of delayed action continues to rob a child of their future.
We cannot allow poverty to be used as an excuse to rob a child of their future.

idioms.definition: A self-reinforcing pattern in which one problem creates the conditions for the same problem to continue.
examples: Child labour and poverty form a vicious cycle that only education can break.
Without decisive action we remain trapped in a vicious cycle of exploitation.
Free schooling is the intervention that breaks the vicious cycle.

idioms.definition: To suffer the delayed consequences of a short-sighted decision.
examples: Societies that tolerate child labour will pay the price later in lost productivity and social unrest.
Every child denied education forces the nation to pay the price later.
We must not force the next generation to pay the price later for our inaction today.

idioms.definition: To deliberately ignore something wrong because it is convenient or profitable.
examples: Consumers who buy cheap goods often turn a blind eye to the child labour behind them.
Governments that fail to enforce laws turn a blind eye to exploitation.
We can no longer turn a blind eye while children work in dangerous conditions.

idioms.idiom: the thin end of the wedge
idioms.definition: A small apparent exception that opens the door to much wider and more serious harm.
examples: Allowing ‘light work’ is often the thin end of the wedge that leads to full exploitation.
Cultural excuses become the thin end of the wedge against children’s rights.
We must reject any exception that serves as the thin end of the wedge.

idioms.definition: To take away the years of safety, play and learning that every child deserves.
examples: Hazardous labour does not merely employ a child; it steals a childhood.
No family hardship can justify the decision to steal a childhood.
The motion exists to stop the practice of those who steal a childhood for profit.

arguments.claim: Child labour permanently damages physical and cognitive development.
arguments.explanation: Children’s bodies and brains are still forming. Long hours of physical work, exposure to dust, chemicals or heavy loads, and chronic exhaustion interrupt normal growth. Studies from brick kilns in South Asia and cocoa farms in West Africa show higher rates of stunting, respiratory disease, and reduced cognitive scores among working children compared with non-working peers. These effects are not temporary. A child who loses critical years of brain development and formal learning enters adulthood with permanently lower earning capacity and poorer health. The short-term income the family gains is therefore purchased at the price of lifelong disadvantage for the child. No society that claims to value its future can accept this trade-off. Immediate abolition, paired with income support and free schooling, is the only way to protect developing minds and bodies.

arguments.claim: Child labour traps families in intergenerational poverty rather than relieving it.
arguments.explanation: When children work instead of attending school they acquire neither literacy nor modern skills. As adults they remain confined to low-paid informal work and are more likely to send their own children to work. Research across Latin America, Africa and South Asia consistently shows that households relying on child labour have lower long-term income trajectories than comparable households that kept children in school. The apparent relief of an extra wage today is outweighed by the loss of future earning power. Countries that enforced compulsory education and removed children from workplaces, such as South Korea in the mid-twentieth century, broke this cycle and achieved rapid economic growth. Tolerating child labour in the name of poverty reduction is therefore self-defeating; it reproduces the very poverty it claims to address.

arguments.claim: Education is the proven pathway out of poverty and child labour blocks that pathway.
arguments.explanation: Every additional year of quality schooling raises lifetime earnings and improves health and civic participation. When a child is removed from school for work, that investment is cancelled. International evidence from conditional cash-transfer programmes in Mexico and Brazil demonstrates that keeping children in school reduces both poverty and child labour simultaneously. The claim that families cannot survive without child wages ignores the fact that many governments and NGOs have successfully replaced those wages with targeted support while expanding school places. The real barrier is political will, not economic impossibility. Abolishing child labour and guaranteeing education is therefore not an attack on the poor; it is the most effective anti-poverty strategy available.

arguments.claim: Hazardous forms of child labour cause irreversible injury and death.
arguments.explanation: Millions of children still work in mining, construction, domestic service under extreme conditions, and agriculture involving pesticides or heavy machinery. These environments produce high rates of injury, chronic illness and premature death. The International Labour Organization documents thousands of work-related fatalities among children each year. No cultural tradition or family hardship can justify placing a twelve-year-old in a gold mine or a brick kiln. Immediate and complete prohibition of hazardous labour is already required by international conventions that most countries have ratified. The continued existence of such work is not a policy disagreement; it is a failure of enforcement and a violation of the most basic duty to protect the vulnerable.

arguments.claim: Consumers and companies share responsibility for the demand that sustains child labour.
arguments.explanation: Global supply chains in garments, cocoa, carpets and electronics still contain significant child labour. When brands and retailers prioritise the lowest possible price, they create the economic incentive for suppliers to use the cheapest workers available—children. Transparent auditing, living-wage requirements, and binding due-diligence laws in importing countries have already reduced child labour in some sectors. The argument that abolition is impossible ignores these successes. Ethical consumption and corporate accountability are not optional extras; they are necessary conditions for ending the practice. Allowing the market to continue using child labour is a collective choice that can and must be reversed.

arguments.claim: Cultural or traditional justifications cannot override universal children’s rights.
arguments.explanation: Appeals to culture or tradition have historically been used to defend many practices later recognised as harmful, from child marriage to caste discrimination. International human-rights instruments establish that children possess rights independent of family or community wishes, including the right to protection from economic exploitation and the right to education. These rights are not Western inventions; they are affirmed by almost every nation through ratification of the Convention on the Rights of the Child. Where tradition conflicts with a child’s safety and development, the child’s rights must prevail. Immediate abolition does not erase culture; it removes only those elements that injure the next generation.

arguments.claim: Gradual approaches have repeatedly failed to protect children.
arguments.explanation: For decades the dominant policy has been ‘progressive elimination’—first remove the worst forms, then address the rest. In practice this has allowed large-scale child labour to continue under the label of ‘light work’ or ‘family assistance’. Data from multiple countries show that the overall numbers of working children decline only when enforcement is strict and education is made genuinely free and compulsory. Soft timelines and exceptions create loopholes that employers exploit. The evidence from countries that moved quickly to ban and enforce, combined with social support, is clearer and more successful. Further delay simply prolongs the harm. Immediate and comprehensive prohibition, backed by resources, is the approach that works.

arguments.claim: Child labour undermines the rule of law and formal employment standards.
arguments.explanation: When children can be employed cheaply and without contracts, adult workers lose bargaining power and formal jobs are undercut. Employers who use child labour gain an unfair cost advantage over those who comply with labour laws. This race to the bottom weakens entire sectors and discourages investment in productivity and skills. Strong enforcement of child-labour bans raises the floor for all workers and encourages businesses to compete on quality and innovation rather than on the exploitation of minors. Far from harming the economy, consistent abolition supports a more stable and productive labour market.

arguments.claim: Girls are disproportionately harmed by child labour and its abolition is a gender-equality measure.
arguments.explanation: In many regions girls are more likely to be withdrawn from school for domestic work, agricultural labour or early marriage linked to economic pressure. The loss of education has lifelong consequences for their health, autonomy and ability to protect their own children. Programmes that remove girls from labour and keep them in school produce measurable gains in delayed marriage, lower fertility, and higher household income in the next generation. Treating child labour as a gender-neutral economic issue ignores this reality. Immediate abolition, with particular attention to girls’ education, is therefore both a child-rights and a women’s-rights priority.

arguments.claim: The existence of successful national examples proves that complete abolition is achievable.
arguments.explanation: Countries at different income levels have demonstrated that child labour can be driven to very low levels through a combination of legal prohibition, free schooling, cash transfers, and enforcement. India’s expansion of the Right to Education and strengthened labour inspections, Brazil’s Bolsa Família programme linked to school attendance, and earlier transformations in East Asia all show rapid declines when political will is present. These cases refute the claim that poverty makes abolition impossible. Where governments decide that children belong in school and back that decision with resources and enforcement, child labour falls. The remaining task is to apply the same determination everywhere rather than accept permanent exceptions.

vocab.definition: The unavoidable reality that some families depend on every available income source simply to eat and survive.
vocab.example: In extreme poverty, economic necessity leaves families with no immediate alternative to children’s contributions.

vocab.definition: The practical choices households make to keep members alive when formal safety nets are absent.
vocab.example: For many rural families, children’s work is a family survival strategy, not a preference.

vocab.definition: The harmful side-effects that appear when a well-intentioned ban is imposed without supporting measures.
vocab.example: Sudden bans without income support produce unintended consequences such as worse exploitation or starvation.

vocab.definition: Age-appropriate tasks that do not interfere with schooling or health and form part of family or community life.
vocab.example: Distinguishing light work from hazardous labour is essential for realistic policy.

vocab.definition: A necessary phase of gradual change that allows families and economies to adjust without catastrophic disruption.
vocab.example: A realistic transition period prevents the social shock of overnight prohibition.

vocab.definition: The informal mechanisms, including children’s earnings, that keep households afloat in the absence of state welfare.
vocab.example: Removing the informal safety net without replacement can push families into deeper crisis.

vocab.definition: The deep integration of children’s participation in work within local traditions of learning and family obligation.
vocab.example: Ignoring cultural embeddedness leads to laws that communities simply disregard.

vocab.definition: The practical impossibility of policing every household and small enterprise in large, poor countries.
vocab.example: An enforcement gap turns absolute bans into paper laws that change nothing on the ground.

vocab.definition: The sudden loss of income and stability that hits families when children’s work is removed without alternatives.
vocab.example: Livelihood disruption can force children into more dangerous hidden forms of labour.

vocab.definition: The recognition that policy must start from actual living conditions rather than abstract ideals alone.
vocab.example: Contextual realism demands that we address poverty first rather than simply outlawing its symptoms.

phrases.phrase: Banning child labour without addressing poverty simply drives it underground.
examples: Banning child labour without addressing poverty simply drives it underground into more dangerous conditions.
Evidence shows that banning child labour without addressing poverty simply drives it underground.
We must avoid a policy where banning child labour without addressing poverty simply drives it underground.

phrases.phrase: Families in extreme poverty do not choose exploitation; they choose survival.
examples: Families in extreme poverty do not choose exploitation; they choose survival with the only options available.
Any honest debate must recognise that families in extreme poverty do not choose exploitation; they choose survival.
Moral lectures ignore the reality that families in extreme poverty do not choose exploitation; they choose survival.

phrases.phrase: A sudden ban without support can make children worse off.
examples: A sudden ban without support can make children worse off by pushing them into street work or trafficking.
History warns that a sudden ban without support can make children worse off.
We cannot risk a situation where a sudden ban without support can make children worse off.

phrases.phrase: Not all children’s work is harmful or exploitative.
examples: Not all children’s work is harmful or exploitative; much of it is light, supervised and compatible with schooling.
Policy must accept that not all children’s work is harmful or exploitative.
Treating every task as equivalent ignores that not all children’s work is harmful or exploitative.

phrases.phrase: Sustainable change requires economic alternatives, not just prohibition.
examples: Sustainable change requires economic alternatives, not just prohibition of existing survival strategies.
The motion fails because sustainable change requires economic alternatives, not just prohibition.
We will achieve more when we accept that sustainable change requires economic alternatives, not just prohibition.

phrases.phrase: Idealism that ignores local realities helps no one.
examples: Idealism that ignores local realities helps no one and often harms the very children it claims to protect.
We must reject idealism that ignores local realities helps no one.
Effective policy begins by recognising that idealism that ignores local realities helps no one.

idioms.idiom: throw the baby out with the bathwater
idioms.definition: To discard something valuable while trying to get rid of something undesirable.
examples: An absolute ban risks throwing the baby out with the bathwater by criminalising light family work along with exploitation.
We must not throw the baby out with the bathwater in our determination to end harmful labour.
Distinguishing harmful from helpful work avoids throwing the baby out with the bathwater.

idioms.idiom: cut off one’s nose to spite one’s face
idioms.definition: To take action that harms oneself more than the intended target.
examples: Forcing families into deeper poverty by sudden bans is to cut off one’s nose to spite one’s face.
A policy that leaves children hungrier cuts off one’s nose to spite one’s face.
We should avoid measures that cut off one’s nose to spite one’s face.

idioms.definition: Something that appears strong or threatening but has no real power or effect.
examples: An unenforceable absolute ban is merely a paper tiger that changes nothing for working children.
Laws without resources and alternatives remain a paper tiger.
We need more than a paper tiger if we are serious about protecting children.

idioms.idiom: put the cart before the horse
idioms.definition: To do things in the wrong order by focusing on a later step before the foundation is ready.
examples: Demanding immediate abolition before creating income alternatives is to put the cart before the horse.
Effective policy refuses to put the cart before the horse.
We put the cart before the horse when we ban first and plan support later.

idioms.definition: To solve one problem by creating another equally serious problem.
examples: Removing children’s wages without replacement is to rob Peter to pay Paul within the same household.
A ban that increases hunger merely robs Peter to pay Paul.
We must design policy that does not rob Peter to pay Paul.

idioms.definition: To base decisions on actual conditions rather than on idealised assumptions.
examples: Policy makers must live in the real world where millions of families have no safety net.
The motion fails to live in the real world of extreme poverty.
Effective protection begins when we live in the real world rather than in abstract principle alone.

arguments.claim: In extreme poverty, children’s earnings are often essential for family survival.
arguments.explanation: In many of the poorest regions, households live on less than two dollars a day and have no access to unemployment benefits, child allowances or reliable informal credit. The small income a child brings from farm work, street vending or domestic service can be the difference between eating and going hungry. Field studies in parts of South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa repeatedly show that when this income is suddenly removed without replacement, families reduce food intake, pull remaining children from school, or send them into riskier hidden work. The moral desire to end child labour is understandable, but an immediate absolute ban that ignores this survival function can increase suffering. A responsible approach first provides alternative income—through cash transfers, school feeding, or adult employment—before removing the child’s contribution. Without that sequence, the ban becomes an attack on the family’s ability to stay alive.

arguments.claim: Sudden prohibition without support drives children into more dangerous hidden labour.
arguments.explanation: When formal or visible forms of child work are banned overnight, the economic pressure on families does not disappear. Children are often pushed into less visible and more hazardous activities: scavenging, illegal mining, domestic service behind closed doors, or trafficking. Evidence from earlier crackdowns in several countries shows temporary drops in official statistics followed by rises in the worst forms of exploitation. Because hidden work is harder to monitor, the children become more vulnerable, not less. An absolute and immediate ban that is not accompanied by income support, school places, and strong social services therefore risks making the problem worse. Gradual reduction combined with positive alternatives has a better record of moving children into safer situations.

arguments.claim: Not all children’s work is harmful; light, supervised tasks can be compatible with development.
arguments.explanation: International labour standards already distinguish between hazardous child labour and light work that does not interfere with education or health. Helping on a family farm after school, learning a traditional craft under parental supervision, or performing modest household chores has been part of childhood in most societies. Treating every form of work as equivalent to factory exploitation ignores this distinction and criminalises ordinary family life. In many rural communities such tasks teach responsibility, skills and cultural knowledge. Blanket prohibition that fails to separate light from harmful work loses public support and becomes unenforceable. Policy should target the genuinely damaging forms first while allowing age-appropriate participation that does not sacrifice schooling.

arguments.claim: Enforcement capacity in poor countries is limited; absolute bans become empty gestures.
arguments.explanation: Most countries where child labour is widespread have large informal economies, weak labour inspectorates, and limited reach into remote villages. Passing a law that prohibits all child work does not automatically create the thousands of inspectors, the transport, or the judicial capacity needed to enforce it. The result is selective enforcement that often targets the poor while leaving powerful employers untouched, or simply no enforcement at all. Laws that cannot be implemented undermine respect for the legal system and leave children no better protected. A more effective strategy concentrates scarce enforcement resources on the worst forms—mining, trafficking, commercial sexual exploitation—while building the economic and educational conditions that reduce the need for child work. Symbolic total bans that exist only on paper help no one.

arguments.claim: Historical development in today’s rich countries involved long transitions, not overnight abolition.
arguments.explanation: The industrialised nations that now condemn child labour themselves passed through periods when children’s work was common. Reduction occurred gradually as wages rose, schooling expanded, and social protection improved. Expecting the poorest countries to achieve in a few years what took others generations, and to do so without similar rises in income, is unrealistic. Imposing an immediate absolute standard without the accompanying economic transformation risks social disruption and resistance. Learning from history means supporting the same sequence—rising adult incomes, accessible education, and progressive restriction of the most harmful work—rather than demanding an instantaneous leap that material conditions do not yet allow.

arguments.claim: Cultural and family contexts shape the meaning of children’s work and cannot be ignored.
arguments.explanation: In many communities, children’s participation in work is understood as part of socialisation, contribution to the household, and preparation for adult roles. External laws that treat all such participation as exploitation can be perceived as an attack on family authority and cultural identity. When communities reject the law as foreign or impractical, compliance collapses. Effective protection works with local understandings, strengthens the positive elements of family work, and focuses enforcement on clear cases of harm and coercion. Top-down absolute prohibition that dismisses cultural context often produces only superficial compliance or open defiance, leaving children unprotected.

arguments.claim: Resources spent on unenforceable total bans would achieve more if directed to education and poverty reduction.
arguments.explanation: Every government faces limited budgets. Money devoted to attempting to police millions of small farms, workshops and households could instead expand school places, provide free meals, or fund cash transfers that make school attendance possible. Evidence from conditional cash-transfer programmes shows that when families receive reliable support linked to education, child labour falls and school enrolment rises. Prioritising an absolute legal ban over these proven interventions is a misallocation of scarce resources. The goal of reducing harmful child work is better served by attacking its root causes—poverty and lack of schooling—than by expanding a legal prohibition that cannot be implemented.

arguments.claim: An absolute ban can increase the risk of child trafficking and commercial exploitation.
arguments.explanation: When legitimate local work opportunities for children are closed without alternatives, some families become more vulnerable to traffickers who promise income elsewhere. Documented cases from several regions show that crackdowns on visible child labour have sometimes been followed by rises in cross-border movement of children into domestic service, begging rings, or sexual exploitation. The most marginalised families, lacking information and protection, are the easiest targets. A policy that removes existing, if imperfect, local options without creating safer ones can therefore enlarge the pool of children at risk of the worst forms of exploitation. Careful sequencing and strong social protection are required to avoid this perverse outcome.

arguments.claim: Sustainable elimination requires rising adult wages and social protection, not legal decree alone.
arguments.explanation: Child labour declines most reliably when adult earnings rise enough that families no longer need children’s income, and when schools are free, accessible and of acceptable quality. Legal bans play a supporting role once those conditions begin to exist. Focusing political energy on an immediate absolute prohibition distracts from the harder, longer-term work of economic development, formal job creation, and building welfare systems. Countries that have made the greatest progress combined legal measures with broad-based growth and education investment. Treating the law as the primary instrument reverses the proven order of change and risks disappointing results.

arguments.claim: The motion’s absolute language leaves no room for the practical, sequenced strategies that have actually worked.
arguments.explanation: Successful reductions in child labour have almost always involved clear priorities: first remove children from the most hazardous sectors, expand schooling, provide income support, and only then tighten restrictions on lighter forms of work. An immediate and exception-free ban rejects this evidence-based sequencing in favour of a single dramatic gesture. In practice, governments that attempt the absolute approach either fail to enforce it or create new hardships. A more honest and effective position accepts that elimination is the goal, recognises the constraints of poverty and capacity, and designs a realistic pathway that protects children at every step rather than risking greater harm in the name of purity of principle.
